P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: No. As an EU member state, Czech Republic applies Article 63 TFEU, which prohibits restrictions on capital movements and payments between EU countries and with non-EU countries. Banks still apply AML/KYC checks and may ask for the source of funds.

P2_fcy_account.answer: Very likely yes: Article 63 TFEU removes capital-movement restrictions, and EU banks and e-money institutions commonly offer foreign-currency or multi-currency accounts. No Czech Republic-specific source on account rules was captured.

L1_registration.question: Must an individual register a business to sell digital services/products? Simplest legal form?
L1_registration.answer: Most freelance services are 'trades' under the Trade Licensing Act, so you need a trade licence (živnostenský list) and become an OSVČ (self-employed person). Apply at any Trade Licence Office (živnostenský úřad), one of the 15 Points of Single Contact, by mail, or electronically with a verified e-signature or BankID. Documents: the Single Registration Form, a criminal record certificate, ID or passport, proof of qualification for regulated trades, and the owner's consent for the business premises. There is a CZK 1,000 administrative fee. You must be 18 with a clean criminal record; formation takes about 1–5 days (Expats.cz).

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: The standard VAT rate is 21%. National threshold: you become a VAT payer from 1 January of the next year once your turnover in Czechia exceeds CZK 2,000,000 in a calendar year, or from the day after it exceeds CZK 2,536,500 (Financial Administration, rules from 2025; Deloitte 2026). The EU SME scheme caps national thresholds at EUR 85,000. PwC: persons seated in the Czech Republic whose turnover exceeds CZK 2 million in a calendar year must register as VAT payers. Where services are taxed (EU-wide rules, illustrated by Irish Revenue guidance): (1) B2B, meaning services to business customers in other EU countries or outside the EU, are taxed where the customer is established, so no Czech Republic VAT is charged; EU business customers self-account under the reverse charge. (2) B2C services to private individuals are, as a rule, taxed where the supplier is established, so Czech Republic VAT applies once you are VAT-registered. (3) Exception: consultancy, legal, accounting, engineering, data-processing, advertising, licensing and electronically supplied services to private customers outside the EU are outside EU VAT, subject to 'use and enjoyment' rules. Electronically supplied services to private customers in other EU countries follow special OSS rules (not captured here).

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law applicable to a small online business
L5_data_protection.answer: The EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies directly in Czech Republic, supervised by the national data protection authority. It covers EU businesses and non-EU businesses offering goods or services to people in the EU.

L6_consumer_ecommerce.question: Consumer-protection / e-commerce rules for online sales (refunds, disclosures)
L6_consumer_ecommerce.answer: EU consumer law gives a 14-day withdrawal right for online and distance purchases without justification: 14 days from delivery for goods, and from conclusion of the contract for services. Exceptions include personalised goods, perishables and date-specific services.

sources.title: Returns and the right of withdrawal (Your Europe)
sources.quote: For goods this means 14 days from the date of delivery, for services 14 days after the day the contract was agreed.

L7_incentives.question: Legal incentives / tax holidays / special zones relevant to small digital businesses
L7_incentives.answer: The flat-rate regime (paušální režim) lets self-employed people (OSVČ) with income up to CZK 2 million pay one monthly amount covering income tax, social and health insurance, in three bands. Band I was CZK 9,984/month, reduced to CZK 9,162 from July 2026; Band II CZK 16,745; Band III CZK 27,139. No expense deductions or tax credits apply. Separately, the 2026 minimum social insurance advance (main activity) is CZK 5,005/month from July 2026.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: none of the major platform barriers apply. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) Physical or digital goods on Etsy (Etsy seller payments are available here). (6) Client payments by PayPal (on PayPal's Payouts list as 'Send, receive, and withdraw in local currency'). (7) Stripe accepts merchants here, so you can take card payments directly on your own site. (8) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
